unit.title: Perpetual Review
unit.summary: Mixed retrieval across the whole course: daily, weekly, boss, term and sweep templates for spaced practice.

lessons.title: Daily Bite
lessons.objective: Review one card from your due concepts.

payload.prompt: After the serve and return bounce, who may volley?

options.text: Only the serving team
Only the receiving team
Either team
Nobody until a third bounce

explanation.correct: Once both the serve and return have bounced, either team may volley freely.
explanation.incorrect: After two bounces, everyone is free to volley anywhere outside the kitchen.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two bounces, then everyone can volley.

payload.prompt: Complete the dink definition.
payload.template: A dink is a {{shot-type}} shot that lands in the {{location}}.

explanation.correct: Dinks are soft shots that land in the opponent's kitchen, a key strategy in pickleball.
explanation.incorrect: Dinking is the soft game: the ball is hit gently and lands in the opponent's kitchen zone.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft shot, opponent's kitchen. That's a dink.

payload.prompt: Match the terms.

pairs.definition: Hitting the ball before it bounces while standing in the non-volley zone.
A soft defensive shot that neutralizes pace and lands in the kitchen.
A ball high enough to hit down at aggressively.

explanation.summary: A kitchen volley is a fault, a reset is a soft defensive shot, and an attackable ball is one high enough to hit down.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kitchen volleys are faults, and resets save you from attacks.

payload.prompt: When is a ball attackable?

options.text: When it bounces on your side
When it's high enough to hit down at
When your opponent hits softly
Only at the net

explanation.correct: Attackable means the ball is high enough (above net height) to hit aggressively downward.
explanation.incorrect: You attack when the ball pops up high enough to hit down. That's your chance.
explanation.sayThisLine: High ball means attackable. Time to speed up.

payload.prompt: The net is exactly the same height all the way across. True?

choices.label: No, it dips lower in the middle

explanation.correct: The net is 36 inches at the posts and 34 inches at the center, so it dips a little in the middle.
explanation.incorrect: It is not level. The net is 36 inches at the posts and sags to 34 inches at the center.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's 36 inches at the posts and 34 in the middle.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I finally hit a clean overhead on their lob. It felt amazing.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: She smashed a high ball downward from above her head.
She served overhand.
She hit the ball into the net from above.
She threw her paddle over the net.

payload.translation: An overhead is a smash: when the opponents lob the ball high, you hit it down hard from above your head.

followUps.line: Did it win you the point?
followUps.why: A simple question that lets her tell the story.

followUps.line: Is a clean one rare at your level?
followUps.why: Shows you know overheads can be tricky to time.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You only need to know an overhead is a smash on a high ball. Ask her about the moment.

lessons.title: Weekly Mix
lessons.objective: Three-round session sampled across concepts you find harder.

payload.prompt: What's a foot fault on the serve?

options.text: Standing on or past the baseline before hitting
Stepping into the kitchen
Hitting the ball too hard
Missing the ball entirely

explanation.correct: A serve foot fault is stepping on or over the baseline (or into the court) before the ball is struck.
explanation.incorrect: Stay behind the baseline when you serve. Touching the line or stepping into the court before you hit is a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot fault means a foot on or over the baseline when you serve.

payload.prompt: A toe touching the kitchen line while volleying is a fault.

scene.alt: Foot position at kitchen line during volley.

explanation.correct: For volleys, the kitchen line counts as part of the kitchen. A toe on the line is a fault.
explanation.incorrect: The line is kitchen. Even touching it while volleying is a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: The kitchen line is part of the kitchen for the volley rule.

payload.prompt: Your team served and they returned deep. What is the smart third shot?

situation.narrative: You served from the baseline and the return landed deep, while the returners are racing up to the kitchen line.

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: Back at the baseline after serving

facts.label: Their position
facts.value: Moving up to their kitchen line

options.label: Soft drop into their kitchen
options.consequence: Right. A drop gives your team time to walk up to the kitchen line without being attacked.

options.label: Hard drive at them
options.consequence: Risky. They are already at the line, so a hard drive comes back at you fast while you are still at the baseline.
considerations: They are set at the net
A drop would give you time

payload.expertNote: Third-shot drop philosophy: patience buys time to reach the net. A drive can work when returners are caught deep, not when they are already set.

payload.title: Her partner bangs everything
payload.setting: Sam is venting about her doubles partner's hard-hitting style.

exchanges.theirMessage: My doubles partner bangs every single ball. It's exhausting to play with.

replies.text: Is that just how they like to play? How do you handle it?
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, it's their style. I try to set up balls they can attack.
replies.coachNote: You asked about both the style and how she copes.
Sympathetic, but a question would keep her talking.

replies.text: Bangers are just bad at pickleball.
replies.theirResponse: They're actually really good. It's just not my style.
replies.coachNote: Do not trash a playing style you just learned about.

exchanges.theirMessage: We win more when they hold back, though. It's a weird balance.

replies.text: So patience wins the long rallies, but they love the big swing?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. Finding the middle is the hard part.
replies.coachNote: You reflected her point and showed you understood the two styles.
Too short to keep the conversation alive.

payload.closingNote: Bangers win with pace and dinkers win with patience. When she vents about a partner's style, ask how she handles it.

payload.prompt: Complete the scoring summary.
payload.template: In side-out scoring only the {{who}} scores, games usually go to {{points}}, and you must win by {{margin}}.

explanation.correct: Only the serving side can score, games usually go to 11, and the winner needs a two-point margin.
explanation.incorrect: In side-out scoring the serving side scores, a standard game goes to 11, and you need to win by 2.
explanation.sayThisLine: Only the serving side scores, to 11, win by 2.

payload.prompt: Why does a team want to reach the kitchen line after the third shot?

options.text: From there they can volley and control the pace of the dinks.
The baseline is out of bounds after the serve.
The kitchen line earns bonus points.
The rules require the serving team to stand there.

explanation.correct: At the kitchen line you can volley, pressure the opponents and control the dink rally, which is why teams walk up after the drop.
explanation.incorrect: It is about position, not rules or points. The kitchen line is the strongest spot because you can volley and take time away from your opponents.
explanation.sayThisLine: Get to the line, and you control the point.

payload.prompt: Unsure if their shot landed out on your side? Calling it out is safest. True?

choices.label: Yes, out is the safe call

explanation.correct: Right. The benefit of the doubt goes to the opponent, so if you cannot tell, the ball is good.
explanation.incorrect: If you are not sure a ball was out, it is in. Giving the opponent the benefit of the doubt is the fair and expected call.
explanation.sayThisLine: If I'm not sure, it's good.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Their lob went right over me, so we switched mid-point.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: She and her partner swapped sides during the rally to cover the lob.
They changed paddles during the point.
They switched to rally scoring.
They replaced a teammate.

payload.translation: Switching means partners trade sides during a rally, often to cover a lob or keep a strong side in place.

followUps.line: Did you call it out loud?
followUps.why: A specific question about communication between partners.

followUps.line: Do you switch a lot, or only on lobs?
followUps.why: Invites her to describe her habits.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need the footwork. Ask her how it worked out.

lessons.title: Kitchen and Score Boss
lessons.objective: Mastery check: the two most-misunderstood areas (kitchen momentum and scoring logic).

payload.prompt: You volley from outside the kitchen, but your paddle tip taps the kitchen floor on the follow-through. Legal?

scene.alt: Paddle tip touching the kitchen after a volley.

explanation.correct: It is a fault. Anything you are holding or wearing touching the kitchen during or right after a volley counts, even if your feet stayed outside.
explanation.incorrect: Feet are not the only thing that counts. Your paddle touching the kitchen surface after a volley is a fault too.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's not just your feet. The paddle counts too.

payload.prompt: At the start of a game, the first serving team gets two servers before a side out. True?

scene.alt: Starting score for a new game.

explanation.correct: Right. The first serving team starts as server number two, so the score is called 0-0-2 and one fault gives the serve to the other team.
explanation.incorrect: Only the very first serving team gets the exception: they start at 0-0-2, as server number two, so they get a single turn before a side out.
explanation.sayThisLine: We start at 0-0-2, so it's one server for us.

payload.prompt: The score is 6-4-1. Where does server 1 stand?

situation.narrative: The serving team's score is 6, and you need to know which side to serve from.

facts.label: Question
facts.value: Even or odd means which side?

options.label: Right service box
options.consequence: Correct. Six is even, so the server stands on the right. Even right, odd left.

options.label: Left service box
options.consequence: No. Even scores serve from the right, and odd scores from the left.

payload.expertNote: Even right, odd left. The serving team's own score decides the side.

payload.prompt: You volley 2 feet outside the kitchen line and the ball lands in. Legal?

explanation.correct: Volleying from outside the kitchen is legal, even if the ball lands in the kitchen.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen rule is about where you stand, not where the ball lands. As long as you volley from outside, the ball can land anywhere in.
explanation.sayThisLine: Where I stand matters, not where the ball lands.

payload.prompt: Your team served and they returned it. Can you volley the return before it bounces?

options.text: Yes, the serve already bounced
No, the return has to bounce first
Only if you served with a drop serve
Only if you are at the net

explanation.correct: The return must bounce on the serving team's side before anyone volleys. Volleying it is a fault.
explanation.incorrect: Two-bounce rule: the serve bounces, the return bounces, and only then can anyone volley. Serve type and position do not change that.
explanation.sayThisLine: The serve bounces, the return bounces, then volleys are fair game.

payload.prompt: Complete the kitchen rule.
payload.template: In the kitchen you may hit a ball after it has {{state}}, but you may not {{action}} it.

explanation.correct: You can stand in the kitchen to hit a ball that has bounced. What you cannot do is volley, hitting the ball in the air, while touching it.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is about volleys. A ball that has bounced can be hit from inside the kitchen, but a volley from there is a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: I can step in to hit a bounced ball. I just can't volley from there.

lessons.title: Term Blitz
lessons.objective: Playbook term drill: identify and define key vocabulary.

payload.prompt: Match the showy shots.

pairs.definition: Jumping from outside the kitchen to volley the ball near the net post.
A shot that goes around the net post rather than over it.
A player crosses behind their partner to hit a ball on the partner's side.

explanation.summary: An Erne is a jump around the kitchen, an ATP goes around the post, and a Bert is running behind your partner to take their ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: Erne and ATP go around the kitchen or post, and Bert is behind the partner.

payload.prompt: Complete these shot and position definitions.
payload.template: An {{shot}} is hit from overhead when the ball is {{height}}. Ready position is {{pos}}.

options: paddle up, knees bent, ready to move
gaps.correct: paddle up, knees bent, ready to move

explanation.correct: A smash is an overhead shot on a high ball, and ready position is an athletic stance with the paddle up.
explanation.incorrect: An overhead smash is hit on a high ball, and ready position means paddle up, knees bent and weight forward so you can move.
explanation.sayThisLine: Paddle up, ready to react, and smash the lobs.

payload.prompt: Match positioning and movement terms.

pairs.definition: Both partners start on the same side to keep strengths aligned.
One partner crosses to intercept the opponent's ball meant for the other.
A small hop as the opponent hits, pushing to react in any direction.

explanation.summary: Stacking is a formation, poaching is an interception, and the split step is footwork as the opponent hits.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack to start, split step as they hit, and poach when the ball is there.

payload.prompt: Complete the MLP tiebreak definition.
payload.template: An MLP {{term}} is a rally-scoring tiebreak to {{points}} when a match is {{tied}}.

explanation.correct: The DreamBreaker is MLP's rally-scoring tiebreak to 21, played when a match is tied 2-2 after four games.
explanation.incorrect: An MLP match is four games, so the tie is 2-2. The tiebreak is the DreamBreaker, played to 21 with rally scoring.
explanation.sayThisLine: DreamBreaker: rally scoring to 21 after a 2-2 tie.

payload.prompt: Match the rec-night terms.

pairs.definition: The line of paddles showing who plays next at open play.
A format where every player or team plays each of the others.
A ranked list where you move up by beating players above you.

explanation.summary: The paddle stack sets the order at open play, round robins let everyone play everyone, and ladders rank you by beating people above you.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack for open play, round robin for everybody, ladder for bragging rights.

lessons.title: Pro and Fan Sweep
lessons.objective: Mixed review of pro, gear, debate, path and season concepts.

payload.prompt: Her MLP team lost in the DreamBreaker. What was the match tied at before it?

options.text: 2-2 in games
3-1 in games
1-0 in games
It is never tied

explanation.correct: A DreamBreaker only happens when the four games finish 2-2, so that is where the match stood.
explanation.incorrect: The four games are women's, men's and two mixed. Only a 2-2 split goes to a DreamBreaker; any other score ends the match.
explanation.sayThisLine: It was 2-2, so the DreamBreaker decided everything.

payload.prompt: Order how a typical pro rally unfolds.

items.text: Serve goes diagonally into the box
Return lands deep after the bounce
Third-shot drop lands in the kitchen
Both teams trade dinks at the line
Someone gets a high ball and speeds it up

explanation.sayThisLine: Serve, return, drop, dinks, then someone attacks.
explanation.correct: A pro rally opens with the serve and return, settles with the third-shot drop and a dink battle, and ends when someone gets an attackable ball.
explanation.incorrect: The order follows the game: serve, return, third-shot drop, dink rally at the kitchen line, then an attack on the first ball that comes up high.

payload.prompt: Quieter paddles and sound barriers are ways communities try to reduce pickleball noise. True?

explanation.correct: Yes. Communities use quieter paddles and balls, sound barriers, location choices and limited hours to keep courts open and neighbors happier.
explanation.incorrect: There are real options: quieter gear, barriers, placement away from homes and quiet hours. The noise debate is about choosing among them.
explanation.sayThisLine: There are fixes. Quiet hours and sound barriers help.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: The draw just dropped and I'm already nervous about her bracket.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The bracket for the event was just published, and she is looking at her player's path.
She dropped her paddle.
The event was cancelled.
She knocked over the paddle stack.

payload.translation: The draw is the published bracket. She is nervous because she can see who her favorite will face.

followUps.line: Who's in the tough part of the draw?
followUps.why: Shows you know a draw has a hard side and an easy side.

followUps.line: Is it a good draw or a scary one?
followUps.why: Lets her tell you how she feels about it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You only need to know the draw is the bracket. Ask her to walk you through the tough matchups.

payload.prompt: Complete the amateur circuit statement.
payload.template: An APP event mixes {{who}} brackets, and divisions are usually split by skill and {{other}}.

explanation.correct: The APP circuit includes both amateur and pro brackets, and divisions are commonly split by skill level and age group.
explanation.incorrect: The APP is not pro-only. Its events include amateur and pro brackets, and divisions group players by skill and often age.
explanation.sayThisLine: The APP has amateur and pro brackets, split by skill and age.

lessons.title: Conversation Sweep
lessons.objective: Mixed review of rec-night language and listening skills.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We're doing a round robin tonight, so I'll get to play everyone.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Every player or team rotates through and plays each of the others.
A knockout where losers go home early.
Only the winners keep playing.
A practice drill with no scoring.

payload.translation: A round robin is a format where everyone plays everyone else, so nobody is knocked out early.

followUps.line: So you don't get eliminated? That sounds fun.
Who are you most excited to play?
followUps.why: Invites her to share the social side.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You only need the basic idea. Ask how they decide the pairings.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: My partner poached three balls in a row. I barely got to hit.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her partner kept crossing over to hit balls that were going to her.
Her partner kept stealing her paddle.
Her partner kept serving out of turn.
Her partner kept calling lines out.

payload.translation: Poaching is stepping across to hit a ball meant for your partner. Sometimes it is a smart move, and sometimes it leaves the partner frustrated.

followUps.line: Did you two talk about it, or did it just happen?
followUps.why: Asks about the partner dynamic without judging.
A light question that lets her vent and laugh.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Poaching can be good or annoying depending on the moment. Ask how she felt about it.

payload.title: She apologizes for gushing
payload.setting: Sam realizes she has been talking about pickleball for a while.

exchanges.theirMessage: Sorry, I've been talking about pickleball for ten minutes straight.

replies.text: Don't apologize. Which part are you most excited about?
replies.theirResponse: Honestly, getting my drop to land. I've finally got it working.
replies.coachNote: You welcomed her passion and asked a question.
Polite, but it closes the door a little.
Never make her feel her passion is too much.

exchanges.theirMessage: My friends stopped asking about my games a while ago.

replies.text: I'm asking. Tell me about your last game.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, so we were down 9-4 and then... you don't mind?
replies.coachNote: You offered genuine interest, and it gave her permission to share.
Sympathetic, but you could have offered to listen.

replies.text: Well, it is hard to follow if you don't play.
replies.coachNote: It explains the friends, but it does not include her.

payload.closingNote: When she worries she talks too much about pickleball, say you want to hear it. Curiosity is the point.

payload.prompt: She uses a term you don't know mid-story. What do you do?

situation.narrative: She is telling a story and says a pickleball word you have never heard.

facts.label: What happened
facts.value: An unfamiliar term in the middle of a story

options.label: Note it and ask at a natural pause
options.consequence: She happily explains, and you kept her story flowing. Asking shows you care enough to get it right.

options.label: Stop her right away and ask what it means
options.consequence: She will explain, but you may break her momentum. It works if you keep it short.

options.label: Nod along and pretend you understood
options.consequence: You may miss the point of the story, and if she asks you something about it, you will be caught.

payload.expertNote: Saying 'what does that mean?' at a natural pause is honest and warm. She will enjoy teaching you.

payload.prompt: On a ladder, you move up by beating players ranked above you. True?

choices.label: Yes, beat them to move up

explanation.correct: Right. A ladder is a ranked list, and you climb by beating players above you.
explanation.incorrect: A ladder is not random. It is a ranking, and you move up by winning challenge matches against players above you.
explanation.sayThisLine: On a ladder you climb by beating the people above you.
